messages.subject: Running SEM without raw data
parts:
My professor told me that he could check whether the raw data is valid or not by "reverse-engineering" the correlation table and standard deviation of each variable(I guess we can make a co-variance table by simple calculation). 
I learnt that we can "reverse" the table to do path analysis by running SEM, but is it possible to "reverse" the table to do regression? http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cov.html I have gone through this website to gain some idea and tried to replicate this to some journal in my field. Should we take the "regression" part of the result to check its data validity? 
There is a website that let everyone anonymously comment on any journal whether the result is correct or not. It seems that they use stata to "reverse" the data back. Can we use lavaan functioning like stata?

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Running SEM without raw data
parts: What I want to see is can we stimulate
replicate?  simulate?
the values in table 2 (e.g. Betas in different regression steps) based on the information from table 1? (unknown information in this case)

Normally, yes, it would be easy to input the vector of correlations and vector of SDs into lavaan's getCov() function to obtain the covariance matrix, then pass it as summary data to fit the model in lavaan() (as you saw here: http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cov.html ).  But because there are moderators, it is not possible to estimate the effect of product-terms (used as additional predictors to estimate interaction effects) without raw data.  

Is this what you mean by trying to simulate data from the covariance matrix, so that you have raw (simulated) data?  That is possible.  Just use the getCov() function to obtain your covariance matrix, then pass it as Sigma to the mvrnorm() function in the MASS package (also pass a mean vector of zeros).  You can generate many (e.g., 100) data sets, then for each data set, fit your regression model(s) and save the results from Table 2 you are interested in reproducing.  You will have a distribution of results (100 values for each value in Table 2), but you can look at the mean to see if the results match closely.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

TC,
  Another way to look at this is that it is good reporting practice to facilitate replication of your analysis.  So, if your analysis requires product variables, it is good reporting practice to always include those in the covariance matrix that you provide in the report.  By following such practices, we optimize the mechanisms of error correction and thus promote scientific progress.

Keith
